passage_title: Salinity, Food, and Light in Pelluna Ciliate Cultures
passage:
Pelluna is a single-celled freshwater ciliate that feeds on algae. Biologists grew Pelluna in glass flasks to see how salinity (dissolved salt, in parts per thousand, ppt), the kind of alga supplied as food, and the daily light period affected the cultures.

Every flask began with 100 Pelluna cells per milliliter (cells/mL) and was kept at 20°C. After 5 days, the biologists recorded the cell density and the average cell length of the Pelluna in each flask (see Table 1).

Experiment 1
Flasks were fed the alga Ternia at salinities of 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8 ppt. Each flask received 12 hours of light per day.

Experiment 2
Flasks were fed the alga Vosk at the same five salinities. Each flask received 12 hours of light per day.

Experiment 3
Flasks were fed Ternia at 4 ppt and received 6, 12, or 18 hours of light per day. (The 12-hour result is that of Experiment 1 at 4 ppt.)
prompt: In Experiment 2, the cell density after 5 days was greatest at which salinity?
explanation: Vosk densities: 410 (0 ppt), 880 (2 ppt), 1,090 (4 ppt), 1,240 (6 ppt), 1,020 (8 ppt). The greatest is 1,240 cells/mL at "6 ppt".
subskill: locate a maximum within one series
topic_tag: Salinity, Food, and Light in Pelluna Ciliate Cultures

passage_title: Catalyst, Humidity, and Curing of Varex Sealant
passage:
Varex is a liquid sealant that hardens after a small amount of catalyst is stirred in. Materials engineers measured how catalyst concentration, air humidity, and temperature affected two properties: set time (the time until the sealant no longer feels tacky) and final hardness after 7 days, measured on a scale from 0 to 100.

Each trial used a 50-gram sample spread 3 mm thick on a steel plate. Table 1 gives the results.

Experiment 1
Catalyst concentration was 0.5%, 1.0%, 1.5%, 2.0%, or 2.5% by mass. Samples cured at 50% humidity and 20°C.

Experiment 2
Samples with 1.5% catalyst cured at 20°C and 20%, 35%, 50%, 65%, or 80% humidity. (The 50% result is that of Experiment 1 at 1.5%.)

Experiment 3
Samples with 1.5% catalyst cured at 50% humidity and 10°C, 20°C, or 30°C. (The 20°C result is that of Experiment 1 at 1.5%.)
prompt: In Experiment 1, final hardness was greatest at which catalyst concentration?
explanation: Experiment 1 hardness: 64, 72, 76, 74, 69 for 0.5% to 2.5%. The greatest, 76, is at "1.5%".
subskill: locate a maximum within one series
topic_tag: Catalyst, Humidity, and Curing of Varex Sealant

consistency_check: Set time falls then levels off with catalyst while hardness peaks at 1.5%; humidity gives a minimum set time at 65% and falling hardness above 50%; the 1.5%/50%/20°C trial is shared by all three experiments with identical values.

passage_title: Ground Cover, Slope, and Grazing at Tollan Ridge
passage:
At Tollan Ridge, a hillside pasture, soil scientists measured how quickly water from a rainfall simulator soaked into the ground. In each trial, simulated rain fell at 60 millimeters per hour (mm/h) for 1 hour on a 1 m² plot. The scientists recorded the infiltration rate (how fast water entered the soil, in mm/h) and the runoff (the percent of the applied water that flowed off the plot). Table 1 gives the results.

Study 1
Plots with three ground covers (bare soil, short grass, or shrub litter, a layer of fallen leaves and twigs) were tested on slopes of 2°, 8°, and 15°. None of these plots had been grazed for 5 years.

Study 2
Plots of short grass on an 8° slope were grazed for one season by 0, 2, 4, or 6 sheep per hectare before being tested. (The 0-sheep result is that of Study 1 for short grass at 8°.)
prompt: Which Study 1 plot had an infiltration rate closest to 30 mm/h?
explanation: Short grass at 8° measured 31 mm/h (1 from 30); short grass at 15° measured 27 and shrub litter at 15° measured 33 (3 from 30); bare soil at 2° measured 18. So "Short grass on the 8° slope".
topic_tag: Ground Cover, Slope, and Grazing at Tollan Ridge

consistency_check: Infiltration and runoff move in opposite directions in every row; slope matters far more on bare soil than under litter (interaction); grazing losses grow with each step (2, 7, 8 mm/h); the 0-sheep row of Study 2 equals the grass 8° row of Study 1.

passage_title: Why Dunmore Vole Numbers Crash
passage:
In the Harl Valley, numbers of Dunmore voles rise for 3 years and then fall sharply in the 4th year. This 4-year cycle has been recorded for 40 years. In a peak year, voles reach about 300 per hectare; after a crash, about 20 per hectare remain. Ermines (small predators) eat voles, and voles feed mainly on cotton sedge, a grasslike plant. Three scientists explain the crash.

Scientist 1
Predators cause the crash. When voles are plentiful, more young ermines survive, so ermine numbers lag vole numbers by about 1 year: ermines are most numerous in the year after voles peak. By then, ermines eat voles faster than voles can reproduce. The crash begins in late summer, when that year's young ermines start to hunt. Voles in a fenced plot that keeps ermines out would not crash. The condition of the sedge does not affect vole breeding.

Scientist 2
The sedge causes the crash. After voles have eaten more than half of the sedge leaves in an area for two summers in a row, the sedge grows leaves rich in silica the following spring. Silica-rich leaves wear down voles' teeth and provide little nourishment, so females stop breeding. Sedge leaves in a crash year contain about 3 times as much silica as usual. The crash begins in spring. Voles in a fenced plot that keeps ermines out would still crash.

Scientist 3
Crowding causes the crash. When vole numbers first exceed about 250 per hectare, females fight over nest sites; stressed females produce fewer young, and many young die in the nest. The crash begins whenever this density is first passed, in any season. The sedge stays nutritious throughout the cycle, so food is not involved. Voles in a plot kept below 250 per hectare by removing voles would not crash, even with ermines present.
prompt: Which scientist(s) would predict that a crash begins in spring?
explanation: Scientist 2 says "The crash begins in spring." Scientist 1 says late summer, and Scientist 3 says whenever density first passes 250, in any season. So "Scientist 2 only".

passage_title: Why the Cawl Ridge Springs Are Warm
passage:
Water flowing from the Cawl Ridge springs averages 34°C. Rainwater at the site averages 9°C, and ordinary groundwater from a well 1 km away is 11°C. The springs' flow rises about 2 months after the start of each wet season. Three scientists explain why the springs are warm.

Scientist 1
Rainwater sinks along a crack in the rock (a fault) to a depth of about 2 km, where the rock is warm, and then rises back to the surface. The round trip takes about 2 months, which is why flow rises about 2 months after the wet season starts. Because the deep rock stays at the same temperature all year, the water's temperature does not change with the flow. On its long trip, the water dissolves minerals, so it should carry about 900 milligrams of dissolved salts per liter (mg/L).

Scientist 2
A body of hot rock lies only about 300 m below the springs. Rainwater that reaches the hot rock is heated and rises within a few days. The 2-month delay in flow is caused by a layer of clay above the hot rock that slows rainwater on its way down. Gas bubbling out of the springs should contain sulfur gases released by the hot rock.

Scientist 3
Rainwater seeps down to a layer of granite about 600 m deep. This granite is unusually rich in elements that release heat, so it warms the water that flows past it. The longer the water stays in contact with the granite, the warmer it becomes, so the springs should be warmest in the months when flow is lowest.

explanation: Scientist 3 says slower flow means warmer water. Scientist 1 says the temperature does not change with the flow, and Scientist 2 does not connect temperature to flow. So "Scientist 3 only".

passage_title: Why Fenn Wood Has So Few Young Oaks
passage:
In Fenn Wood, Ardel oaks older than 80 years are common, but oaks younger than 20 years are rare: about 3 per hectare, compared with about 60 per hectare in nearby Barrow Wood. The two woods have similar soil and similar numbers of old oaks. Three students explain the shortage of young oaks in Fenn Wood.

Student 1
Deer eat young oaks. Fenn Wood has about 25 deer per square kilometer, compared with about 6 in Barrow Wood. Acorns in Fenn Wood do sprout each spring, but deer eat most of the seedlings before their second summer. Fencing out deer would let seedlings survive.

Student 2
Insects destroy the acorns before they can sprout. In Fenn Wood, more than 90% of acorns on the ground have exit holes left by acorn weevils, compared with about 30% in Barrow Wood. As a result, few seedlings ever sprout in Fenn Wood. Fencing out deer would not increase the number of young oaks.

Student 3
Shade kills the seedlings. Glossbrook, a shrub that has spread through Fenn Wood since 1990, shades the ground. Acorns sprout, but a seedling dies within its first summer if the light reaching the ground is less than 5% of full sunlight; under glossbrook, the light is about 2% of full sunlight. Removing glossbrook would let seedlings survive, even if the deer remain.
prompt: Which student(s) state that acorns in Fenn Wood do sprout?
explanation: Student 1 says acorns "do sprout each spring," and Student 3 says "Acorns sprout." Student 2 says few seedlings ever sprout. So "Students 1 and 3 only".
